overview: The REPORT Act would require federal agencies to explain to Congress and the public what happened after each act of terrorism in the United States. Within one year after the lead agency finishes its investigation, the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Attorney General, the FBI Director, and when appropriate the head of the National Counterterrorism Center would send a joint unclassified report (with an optional classified section) to the homeland security, judiciary, and intelligence committees of both chambers, and post it on a public website. Each report would lay out the known facts, identify security gaps that could be closed to prevent similar attacks, and recommend changes in law or law enforcement practices. Officials could hold back specific information that would endanger an ongoing investigation or prosecution, but must tell Congress they did so, and reports may be combined into a quarterly report. The requirement would end five years after enactment. The bill was placed on the Senate calendar on November 3, 2025, after committee approval without changes.
for: Supporters say routine, public after-action reports would help Congress and the public learn from each attack and spot security gaps, instead of lessons being lost once an investigation closes.
against: Critics say mandatory public reports could add paperwork for already stretched counterterrorism agencies and risk revealing sensitive methods, even with the classified annex and investigation exception.
